extracted.intended_audience: princes, courtiers, nobles, tutors, and readers of Renaissance conduct literature
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on the qualities, virtues, duties, and methods by which a courtier and a prince should be formed and should govern—covering education of virtue, moral psychology, modes of rule, and the ends of law and war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtues are learned, not wholly natural
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral virtues are not in us by nature wholly; we are born capable of receiving them and custom (practice) creates the habit so that we first practise virtue or vice, and then are virtuous or vicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument examples: a stone repeatedly thrown upward will not become naturally inclined to move upward; law presumes virtues can be learned because punishment aims to prevent future error; physicians should not focus only on trivial ailments. Emphasises responsibility and the role of education/practice rather than innate disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a master/instructor to cultivate moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: As in other arts, it is necessary to have a master who, by instruction and good reminders, shall arouse and awake in us those moral virtues whereof we have the seed enclosed and buried in our soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: like a good husbandman cultivating seeds by clearing thorns and tares. The master both teaches and cultivates through studied practice and reason to purify the soul and lift ignorance's veil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish natural gifts from acquired virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Things bestowed by nature (e.g., senses) come into operation before practice and are perfected by training; moral virtues require study and practice to ripen into action and perfect character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: senses first have the power then perform; good masters teach manners (eating, speaking, walking) as well as letters. Implies pedagogical emphasis on habituation and guided training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance is the more perfect virtue for rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance (unperturbed, having extinguished the fire of lust) is very perfect and especially befitting to princes, because from it spring many other virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with continence (an imperfect virtue because it contains a grain of passion) and incontinence (a diminished vice with some reason). Uses military captain analogy: conquering without opposition (temperance) is preferable when genuine. Implies preference for internal harmony rather than mere self-restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate passions; do not extirpate them
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not well to uproot passions entirely; rather temperance should moderate and bring passions into the sway of reason, since passions contain elements of good and when moderated help virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: forbidding wine to avoid drunkenness or forbidding running because one may fall. Positive examples: wrath aiding strength, hatred of evil aiding justice; taming horses—allowing them to run seasonably under control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is the foundational and most perfect virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is described as the 'unspotted virgin, friend of modesty and good, queen of all the other virtues' because other virtues perform their works through it and it benefits both possessor and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice enables correct action and helps all other virtues; a ruler should especially embody justice because the prince's life is law and example to subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foresight (practical judgment) guides the virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide of the virtues is foresight, which consists in a certain judgment in choosing well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foresight is the faculty for prudent selection and is necessary for the chain of virtues (liberality, magnificence, gentleness, affability, etc.). Implies importance of deliberation and good judgment in rulers and courtiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnanimity requires other virtues; it cannot stand alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnanimity enhances other virtues but cannot stand alone; whoever has no other virtue cannot be magnanimous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows a hierarchical dependency among virtues: magnanimity presupposes temperance, justice, foresight, etc., and so must be cultivated alongside them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtier must possess accomplishments that win the prince's favour
rubrics_metrics.description: Accomplishments such as music and dancing (and others) are not of small importance; they help to win the prince's favour, which is necessary before a courtier can instruct the prince in virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: thinking such accomplishments are trivial. Practical guidance: courtiers should cultivate varied accomplishments to gain access and influence; these are instruments enabling moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: The courtier's gift should be instruction in ruling, not material gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: A courtier should give the prince the faculty of ruling rightly—the manner and mode of ruling and reigning—rather than gold, silver, or raiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This faculty is 'perhaps the greatest and rarest' and more valuable than material offerings. Emphasises long-term civic benefits over short-term displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prince should combine contemplative and active lives, privileging contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes ought to lead both lives, but especially the contemplative: one part consists in perceiving rightly and judging, the other in commanding justly; the aim of the active life ought to be the contemplative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Command is the chief office of princes and they must sometimes be present at and partake in execution, but their actions should serve contemplation (peace is the end of war). Encourages informed, deliberative rule rather than pure activism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prince's chief aim: establish laws and ordinances to secure peace and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: The good prince's office is to establish his people under such laws and ordinances that they may live at ease and peace, without danger and with dignity; the end of such regulation is tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failure: states prosperous in war but ruined in peace from inability to enjoy ease. Guidance: legislate and organize society to preserve the benefits of peace, not merely warlike virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: War should not be cultivated for lust of rule; use force only for defence or just causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes ought not to make their people warlike for lust of rule; warlike training is justifiable only to defend against bondage or wrong, to drive out tyrants, to govern maltreated peoples well, or to subdue those by nature deserving rule for their good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative anti-pattern: Scythian customs that rewarded slaying enemies to promote endless domination. Implies ethical limits on military policy and the aim of war as defence or justice, not conquest for pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prince must cultivate virtue in subjects; the people's goodness testifies to the prince's goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: A very great proof that the prince is good is when his people are good, because the prince's life is law and preceptress to his subjects; the prince ought not only to be good but to make others good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the prince like the square used by architects—straight himself and makes straight what he applies to. Practical implication: moral leadership and exemplary conduct are essential duties of rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office and power reveal internal dispositions; power amplifies vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Office shows what men are: corrupt and vicious minds seldom disclose defects except when filled with authority; then they show greed, pride, insolence, tyranny, persecuting the good and exalting the wicked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bias cracked vase example: flaws are revealed when filled. Historical examples: tyrants who lived in fear (Clearchus, Aristodemus). Implies that selection and education for office must guard against latent vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Princes should study wisdom diligently and have reason ingrained
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince must devote every study and diligence to wisdom and set before himself the law of reason, ingraining it so that day and night it may admonish him, freeing him from disturbances of intemperate minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: cultivate internalized standards of reason and justice so they operate inwardly; warns that unchecked power plus ignorance leads to tyranny and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: True liberty is living according to good laws; obedience can be natural and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: True liberty is not to live as we like but to live according to good laws. Obedience is natural and useful in appropriate cases, as some are by nature fit to command and others to obey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political implication: liberty is compatible with lawful order; the book rejects a simplistic individualist conception of freedom and defends ordered liberty under good laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three forms of good government and their corruptions; monarchy preferable if not tyrannical
rubrics_metrics.description: Three modes are monarchy, the rule of the good (optimates), and popular government; each has an opposite extreme (tyranny, oligarchy, rule by rabble), and tyranny is the worst—therefore monarchy, as opposite to the worst, is the best of the three good kinds if it avoids tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical criterion for regime comparison: evaluate forms by their tendencies toward extremes and which extreme is worst. Encourages assessing governments by likely corruptions and relative harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate offices to fit men while retaining supreme authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Discreet and virtuous men may be given offices for which they are fitted so they may command and govern the less wise, but the chief rule should wholly depend upon the supreme prince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical governance: empower capable subordinates to exercise authority appropriate to their talents, but maintain ultimate responsibility and unity of command.
